pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Walk me through one red-green-refactor cycle. What is each phase for, and what does skipping each one cost?
expected_points: red: write one small failing test — an executable spec; skipping it risks tests that never failed and may verify nothing
green: simplest change that passes, nothing speculative; skipping the discipline leaves untested branches in 'tested' code
refactor: improve design while tests stay green as a safety net; skipping it piles up design debt under a passing suite

questions.prompt: You are certain your new test will fail — why run it and watch the red anyway?
expected_points: the red run is the only time the test itself is tested — it can be vacuous, miswired, or asserting the wrong thing
you also check the failure message is the one you expected and would be useful when it fires later
same rule for bugs: reproduce with a failing test before fixing, or the test never proves it would have caught the bug

questions.prompt: Your code depends on a payment gateway. For 'an expired card is declined' versus 'each order is charged exactly once', which double fits each test — fake, stub, or mock/spy — and why?
expected_points: expired-card: a stub returning a canned decline — assert on your code's resulting state, not the interaction
charged-exactly-once: a mock/spy recording calls — the charge call itself is the behavior, there is no state to read back
a fake is a working lightweight implementation (e.g. in-memory store) for broader flows; prefer state-based doubles because interaction tests couple to implementation and break under refactor

questions.prompt: A function calls time.Now() and prints its result to the terminal. Why can't you test it properly, and what is the redesign?
expected_points: time.Now() is a hidden input — the outcome depends on when the test runs; printing is a hidden output the test cannot observe
inject the dependencies: a clock interface or func field for now, and a writer/notifier for output — tests substitute a stub clock and a buffer or spy
this mirrors the exercise: LegacySendOverdue versus Reminder with Clock and Notifier fields

questions.prompt: How does writing the test first change the shape of an API? Give a concrete example where the interface came out different.
expected_points: the test makes you the first consumer: construction, calls, and result-checking get exercised before implementation hardens
a hard-to-write test is a design smell surfacing early — hidden dependencies and missing return values hurt the test immediately
example: sendOverdue test-first grew injected clock/notifier and a count return instead of reaching for the global clock and printing

questions.prompt: A team mocks every collaborator and their tests break on every refactor even when behavior is unchanged. What is the diagnosis and the fix?
expected_points: over-specified interaction tests assert how the code works instead of what it does, coupling tests to the implementation
fix: state-based tests with fakes/stubs for anything with observable results; keep mocks/spies only at boundaries where the call is the behavior

questions.prompt: Is code you don't TDD ever acceptable? Where does the loop fit badly, and what do you do instead?
expected_points: exploratory spikes where the shape is unknown: write throwaway code to learn, then delete it and TDD the keeper
the discipline targets code you intend to keep; the non-negotiable core is never shipping production changes without a test that once failed
